extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy, legal theorists, and rulers/practitioners of governance
extracted.subtask_short: criteria for political and ecclesiastical authority
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and standards for distinguishing law from counsel, for locating lawful jurisdiction and sovereignty (civil vs. ecclesiastical), and for deciding when to obey God or human authorities. The text evaluates claims of papal/spiritual supremacy and sets out conditions under which commands count as binding civil law or merely pastoral counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Law and Counsell
rubrics_metrics.description: That Law, is distinguished from Counsell, in this, that the reason of a Law, is taken from the designe, and benefit of him that prescribeth it; but the reason of a Counsell, from the designe, and benefit of him, to whom the Counsell is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to test whether a command is a binding law (aimed at the prescriber's authority and enforceable with punishments) or merely pastoral/advisory (aimed at the recipient's good, e.g., salvation). Many Apostolic injunctions are treated as counsel because their end is the recipient's salvation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostolic acts as counsel not law
rubrics_metrics.description: The Acts of this Councell, were not Laws, but Counsells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where apostles act to promote salvation and expect reward regardless of obedience, their decrees function as advice rather than enforceable civil law. Treat epistolary injunctions as persuasive moral guidance unless accompanied by civil sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical princes must also be civil sovereigns to be princes
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no Ecclesiasticall Princes but those that are also Civill Soveraignes; and their Principalities exceed not the compasse of their Civill Soveraignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count as 'ecclesiastical princes' only those with civil sovereignty; spiritual authority alone does not create a separate princely jurisdiction that supersedes civil rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excommunication is not equivalent to civil punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not... the Power of a Magistrate to punish offenders, that is meant by a Rod; but onely the Power of Excommunication, which is not in its owne nature a Punishment, but onely a Denouncing of punishment, that Christ shall inflict, when he shall be in possession of his Kingdome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish social/religious sanctions (excommunication, removal of fellowship) from civil penalties (death, imprisonment, fines). Excommunication is a spiritual/social sanction and does not substitute for civil coercive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral commands cannot compel inward belief
rubrics_metrics.description: A Christian King, as a Pastor, and Teacher of his Subjects, makes not thereby his Doctrines Laws. He cannot oblige men to beleeve; though as a Civill Soveraign he may make Laws suitable to his Doctrine, which may oblige men to certain actions, and sometimes to such as they would not otherwise do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of pastoral power: rulers may legislate external actions but cannot lawfully command internal belief. Legislative acts must be justified as civil commands, not conflated with pastoral teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience in apostolic language often means practice/hearkening, not legal compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: The word Obey... signifieth Hearkening To, or Putting In Practice, not onely that which is Commanded by him that has right to punish, but also that which is delivered in a way of Counsell for our good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading religious texts or exhortations, interpret 'obey' contextually: it may prescribe moral practice without implying civil jurisdiction or punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction is the power to hear and determine causes and belongs to civil sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction is the Power of hearing and determining Causes between man and man; and can belong to none, but him that hath the Power to prescribe the Rules of Right and Wrong; that is, to make Laws; and with the Sword of Justice to compell men to obey his Decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this functional test for jurisdiction: ability to make binding rules and to compel obedience (eg, through courts, enforcement) indicates civil jurisdiction; absent civil coercion, a claim of jurisdiction is hollow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bishops derive their jurisdiction from the civil sovereign (except where sovereign)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is thereby signified, that they had their Authority from the Civill Soveraign: and therefore that place proveth, that Bishops in every Christian Common-wealth have their Authority from the Civill Soveraign; and from the Pope in his own Territories only, and not in the Territories of any other State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate episcopal authority by tracing its source: if appointed or authorized by a civil sovereign, their jurisdiction is derivative; papal jurisdiction is limited to territories where the Pope is also civil sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Pope lacks universal direct temporal jurisdiction outside his territory
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pope hath not any Temporall Jurisdiction DIRECTLY [in the Dominions of other Princes].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat papal claims to depose or transfer temporal authority in other states with skepticism: such claims are not direct civil rights unless backed by the consent or sovereignty of those states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil sovereign authority originates from the consent of the governed
rubrics_metrics.description: The Right of all Soveraigns, is derived originally from the consent of every one of those that are to bee governed; whether they that choose him, doe it for their common defence... or whether they doe it, to save their lives, by submission to a conquering Enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legitimacy of civil authority by whether it rests on explicit or tacit consent of the people; contrast this with doctrines claiming immediate divine grant without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of functions does not imply subjection of persons
rubrics_metrics.description: From the Subordination of an Art, cannot be inferred the Subjection of the Professor; so from the Subordination of a Government, cannot be inferred the Subjection of the Governor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate hierarchical relation of roles or ends (e.g., spiritual ends subordinating temporal means) with personal subjection; political obligation must be established on persons and consent, not merely on functional subordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects should not depose their sovereign for perceived heresy (toleration over deposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If they tolerate not their King, whatsoever law hee maketh, though it bee concerning Religion, doe violate their faith, contrary to the Divine Law, both Naturall and Positive... to depose him, when he is chosen, is in no case Just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposition of a sovereign for religious reasons is presented as a violation of covenant/faith; the text argues for toleration of erring sovereigns rather than private or popular usurpation of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical examples do not establish political right
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using precedent or notable cases (e.g., excommunications, depositions) as proof of normative right; assess underlying legal and consent-based principles instead of relying solely on historical acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When two commands conflict, obey God if one is known to be God's
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man receiveth two contrary Commands, and knows that one of them is Gods, he ought to obey that, and not the other, though it be the command even of his lawfull Soveraign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a limiting principle: divine command overrides civil command only when the agent can be certain the command is genuinely from God. The central problem is epistemic — discerning whether a purported divine command is authentic or a misuse of God's name for private ends.
